# Measuring D-efficiency of experiment designs

Make a simple design of experiment for a conjoint survey on cars.

First, define the attributes and levels (the same car survey from class 8):

```{r}
profiles <- cbc_profiles(
  price       = c(15, 20, 25),              # Price ($1,000)
  fuelEconomy = c(20, 25, 30),              # Fuel economy (mpg)
  accelTime   = c(6, 7, 8),                 # 0-60 mph acceleration time (s)
  powertrain  = c('Gasoline', 'Hybrid', 'Electric')
)
```

We'll also need priors - our assumptions about the coefficients. These are the
same priors we used to simulate choices in class 8:

```{r}
priors <- cbc_priors(
  profiles,
  price       = -0.7,
  fuelEconomy = 0.1,
  accelTime   = -0.2,
  powertrain  = c('Hybrid' = 0.5, 'Electric' = -4.0)
)
```

# Random design

Make a random design. Each respondent gets their own independently drawn set of
questions (this is _not_ a full factorial - it randomly samples profiles):

```{r}
design_rand <- cbc_design(
  profiles = profiles,
  n_resp   = 500, # Number of respondents
  n_alts   = 3,   # Number of alternatives per question
  n_q      = 6    # Number of questions per respondent
)

head(design_rand)

cbc_inspect(design_rand)
```

# Bayesian D-efficient design

Make a Bayesian D-efficient fractional factorial design:

```{r}
design_opt <- cbc_design(
  profiles = profiles,
  n_resp   = 500, # Number of respondents
  n_alts   = 3,   # Number of alternatives per question
  n_q      = 6,   # Number of questions per respondent
  priors   = priors,
  method   = 'modfed',
  n_start  = 5,
  n_blocks = 1
)

head(design_opt)

cbc_inspect(design_opt)
```

Tuning parameters:

- `method`: Which design algorithm to use. There are seven:
    - `"random"` (the default): independently sample profiles for each respondent.
    - `"shortcut"`, `"minoverlap"`, `"balanced"`: fast greedy algorithms that
      target attribute balance and low overlap. They do **not** use priors.
    - `"stochastic"`, `"modfed"`, `"cea"`: the D-optimal algorithms. These are
      the ones that minimize D-error. `"modfed"` (modified Federov) swaps whole
      profiles exhaustively; `"cea"` (coordinate exchange) swaps one attribute
      at a time and is faster; `"stochastic"` accepts the first improvement it
      finds and is fastest.
- `priors`: Your assumed coefficients. Provide them and the D-optimal methods
  minimize the $D_p$-error; omit them and they minimize the $D_0$-error (which
  assumes every coefficient is 0).
- `n_start`: Number of random starts when searching for a D-efficient design.
  More starts is a better search, but slower.
- `n_blocks`: Number of blocks the design is split into. More blocks means more
  people see more different questions, which increases overall efficiency, but
  it takes longer to compute.

# Comparing designs

`cbc_compare()` puts the key metrics for any number of designs side by side:

```{r}
cbc_compare(
  Random = design_rand,
  Modfed = design_opt,
  metrics = c("efficiency", "balance", "overlap")
)
```

Notice two things:

1. The D-error columns are `NA` for the random design. {cbcTools} only records a
   D-error for designs built with a D-optimal method, because D-error gets
   computed _during_ the optimization. We'll compute it ourselves below.
2. The random design is actually _more balanced_ than the D-efficient one. That
   is not a bug. Balance and efficiency are different goals, and a D-optimal
   algorithm will happily sacrifice balance to buy information about the
   coefficients you said you care about.

# Computing D-error ourselves

Recall from the slides that the information matrix for one choice question is

$$\boldsymbol{I}_q = \boldsymbol{X}_q^{\top}\left(\text{diag}(\boldsymbol{P}_q) - \boldsymbol{P}_q \boldsymbol{P}_q^{\top}\right)\boldsymbol{X}_q$$

where $\boldsymbol{P}_q$ are the choice probabilities implied by our priors. Sum
over the questions one respondent sees to get $\boldsymbol{I}$, then

$$D = \left|\boldsymbol{I}\right|^{-1/K}$$

where $K$ is the number of coefficients. That's the whole calculation, and it's
short enough to write out:

```{r}
d_error <- function(design, priors = NULL) {
  # Dummy code the design so the columns line up with the coefficients
  design <- cbc_encode(design, coding = "dummy")

  # With no priors, every coefficient is assumed to be 0 (the "D0-error")
  beta <- priors$pars
  if (is.null(beta)) {
    pars <- setdiff(
      names(design),
      c("profileID", "blockID", "respID", "qID", "altID", "obsID", "choice")
    )
    beta <- setNames(rep(0, length(pars)), pars)
  }
  X <- as.matrix(design[, names(beta), drop = FALSE])

  # D-error is a property of the set of questions ONE respondent sees,
  # so compute it separately for each respondent
  blocks <- split(seq_len(nrow(design)), design$respID)
  vapply(blocks, function(rows) {
    info <- matrix(0, length(beta), length(beta))
    for (q in unique(design$obsID[rows])) {
      Xq <- X[rows[design$obsID[rows] == q], , drop = FALSE]
      p  <- exp(Xq %*% beta)
      p  <- as.vector(p / sum(p))
      info <- info + t(Xq) %*% (diag(p) - p %*% t(p)) %*% Xq
    }
    # A block that can't identify the model has a singular information
    # matrix - treat that as infinitely bad rather than NA
    error <- det(info)^(-1 / length(beta))
    if (is.finite(error)) error else Inf
  }, numeric(1))
}
```

Check it against {cbcTools}. Every respondent sees the same block in our
D-efficient design (`n_blocks = 1`), so there is a single D-error to compare:

```{r}
# Ours:
median(d_error(design_opt, priors))  # Dp-error, using the priors
median(d_error(design_opt))          # D0-error, assuming all coefficients are 0

# What cbc_inspect() reported above:
cbc_inspect(design_opt, sections = "efficiency")
```

Now the comparison we actually wanted - the same calculation on the random
design:

```{r}
errors_rand <- d_error(design_rand, priors)
errors_opt  <- d_error(design_opt, priors)

median(errors_rand)
median(errors_opt)
```

The D-efficient design has a much lower D-error, which is the whole point: for
the same 6 questions per respondent, it extracts substantially more information
about the coefficients.

One more thing worth noticing. Because each respondent in a random design gets
their own questions, each one has their own D-error, and some of them are
terrible:

```{r}
summary(errors_rand)

# How many respondents got a block of questions that can't even identify
# the model (an information matrix with no inverse)?
sum(!is.finite(errors_rand))
```

A handful of respondents saw 6 questions from which these 5 coefficients cannot
be estimated at all. The D-efficient design guarantees that never happens,
because every respondent gets the block the algorithm chose.
